Brick 3, step by step

This page shows, with short animations made for this course, everything your team does in Lab 03: the Model Fair, the process decision record, the life-cycle map and the first estimate — then the hour at home. The full conditions are in the lab document; this page is the visual companion.

Time budget 1 – 2 – 11 h lecture · 2 h in class · 1 h at home — at most 3 hours of lab work (2 in class + 1 at home)
Deliverable/docs/03-process.md, tag block3, link and tag on the LMS (Learning Management System)
DueSunday, December 20, 2026, 23:59 — recommended first version block3-draft by Sunday, October 11, 23:59
Weight6.5 % of the course grade, the four Cs: Complete · Correct · Consistent · Clear

How the bricks work from now on

WhenWhat
Odd modulesA new brick: Brick 1 (done) · Brick 3 — today · Brick 5 — October 20 · Brick 7 — November 3 · the Mid-Term, November 17, counts as “Brick 9”
Even modulesLecture as usual; the Studio is coached time to finish the latest brick
December 1, 8, 15Supervised finishing workshops
Sunday, December 20, 23:59Every brick is due

Every tool and technique here is open. The decision-record format, the timeline, the calculator, Git, the hosting site, the editor — each is a suggestion. Replace any of them, combine them, or build your own: a small script, a form, a checklist. Research what you choose — who makes it, its licence and price, where your data goes — and name it in section 0 of your file. Starting points (official sites): Git · GitHub · GitLab · Codeberg · Visual Studio Code · Mermaid · draw.io · Excalidraw · Python.

Before you open a link or install anything, use the checklist of the Legal Notice, section 14 and Annex C: official sites only, links checked with VirusTotal, published checksums verified.

How to use the animations. They play by themselves. Pause freezes the last frame (the complete result), Restart plays from the beginning, a click on an animation enlarges it (on a phone it turns sideways), and the two download buttons save the animation or its last frame for your notes. A red number such as 1 points to a version note: tools change, and a newer version may look different from what you see here.

In class — Studio 1:10–2:50, wrap-up to 3:00

1

Set up

1:10–1:15 · 5 minutes · in class

  1. Open Brick 1 and read your vision sentence aloud once.
  2. Copy 03-process_TEMPLATE.md to /docs/03-process.md — with the command line, your editor or the file manager.
  3. Fill the header: team, product, date, members present. Name today's Scribe and start the timer.

Done when: the file exists in the repository on the right path.

2

The Model Fair

1:15–1:45 · 30 minutes · in class

  1. Prepare (9 min): three arguments for “Why is our model the best process for a campus app built by 3–4 students in one semester?” and the model's biggest honest drawback.
  2. Pitch (3 min; 2 min with five teams or more): one speaker, no slides; end with the drawback.
  3. Rebuttal (1 min; left out with seven teams or more): another team asks one hard question; answer in 30 seconds.
  4. Vote (1 min): a show of hands for fit to the case and honesty about drawbacks — never for your own team.
  5. Copy (2 min) the five items into section 1.

Done when: section 1 holds the model, three arguments, the drawback, the rebuttal with your answer, and the winner.

No photos or recordings of classmates without their permission — Legal Notice, section 17.

3

Process decision record

1:45–2:20 · 35 minutes · in class

  1. Context: at least five checkable facts — hours per member, requirement stability, biggest risk, client availability, fixed dates.
  2. Drivers: 3 to 5 criteria, most important first.
  3. Options: at least three models, two pros and two cons each, for your product.
  4. Decision: “We will use … because …”.
  5. Consequences: at least two gains and two costs, one action per cost; then “We will revisit this decision if …”.

Done when: five facts, three options, one decision sentence, two gains, two costs with actions, a trigger; status Accepted or Proposed.

4

Life-cycle map

2:20–2:40 · 20 minutes · in class

  1. Your phases as bars (increments, or the stages of a linear model).
  2. The bricks and course dates: Bricks 1, 3, 5 (October 20), 7 (November 3) and the Mid-Term (November 17) as milestones; the finishing workshops as one bar (December 1–15); the deadline (December 20) as the last milestone.
  3. The five groups of IEEE Std 1074 (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers Standard 1074), each with a real activity of your project and its date.

Any form: a photographed paper strip or a drawing saved as /docs/img/03-lifecycle.png and shown with ![Life-cycle map](img/03-lifecycle.png), a table, or a Mermaid chart written as text inside the file.

Done when: phases, all bricks and course dates, and five groups are on the map.

5

Numbers: first estimate and the gap

2:40–2:50 · 10 minutes · in class

  1. Size: list the pieces, estimate lines for each, add, divide by 1,000 → S.
  2. Compute with Basic COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model), organic mode: E = 2.4 × S1.05 person-months · D = 2.5 × E0.38 months · P = E ÷ D people, every intermediate number shown (31.05 = 3.17), one decimal.
  3. Compare with your capacity (members × hours a week × weeks; 152 hours = one person-month). The course rhythm gives the project 100 minutes of Studio and 120 minutes of Home Sprint a week — this lab's hour at home is part of it. Write one gap sentence.

Done when: size list, three numbers with working, capacity, one gap sentence.

2:50

Wrap-up

2:50–3:00 · 10 minutes · in class

Exit ticket, one sentence on paper: “Which model did your team choose, and what is its biggest drawback?” Push the draft before you leave — the same commands as in Step 9, without the tag.

At home — 60 minutes, maximum

6–8

Finish, check twice, decide

35 minutes · at home

  1. Step 6 (15 min): read the decision record as a stranger would — every fact checkable, every weakness of the model in the consequences, adjectives replaced by facts.
  2. Step 7 (10 min): the map has every brick, the Mid-Term, December 20 and the five groups; a Mermaid chart must be drawn on the hosting site (an error message names the line to fix).3
  3. Step 8 (10 min): recompute E, D and P with a second tool, put your capacity in person-months, and write one scoping decision — cut, postpone or simplify. It is the first input of Brick 5.

Done when: every box of the checklist is ticked.

9

Commit, tag, push, post

10 minutes · at home

  1. Commit and push the file: git add docs/ → git commit -m "…" → git push.1
  2. git push does not send tags, so each tag is pushed by name. Optional first version for feedback (recommended by Sunday, October 11, 23:59): git tag block3-draft then git push origin block3-draft.
  3. Graded version — tag it last, when the brick is final, by Sunday, December 20, 2026, 23:59: git tag block3 then git push origin block3. Both tags may point at the same commit; if you change the file after tagging block3, run git tag -f block3 and git push --force origin block3. If only block3-draft exists on December 20, that version is graded.
  4. Check the tag on the hosting site (on GitHub: Releases → Tags).2 Then post the repository link and the tag name on the LMS (Learning Management System) — for the draft if you want feedback, and for the final version.6

Declare any AI (Artificial Intelligence) tool in section 0 of your file, and keep every name and example fictional — Legal Notice, sections 6.7, 18.1 and 18.2.

10

Read and memorise

15 minutes · at home

  • Pressman and Maxim, Software Engineering: A Practitioner's Approach, 9th edition (McGraw Hill): skim the sections of chapter 2 on the models you did not defend today and the estimation pages of chapter 25; the rest of chapters 2 and 4 belongs to your weekly reading, outside this hour.
  • The ten flash-cards of the week: process flow · umbrella activity · IEEE Std 1074 (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers Standard 1074) · Waterfall · V-model · incremental model · prototyping · spiral model · Unified Process · COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model).
  • Optional, never graded: the three practice sizes of the schedule (2, 8 and 20 thousand lines) in /docs/numbers.md.

That is the hour. If you are past it, stop: what is missing becomes a question for the coached Studio of October 13.

Build your own tool — one possible example

The lab asks you to compute E, D and P twice, with two different tools. Here is one way to make the second tool yourself: a short Python script, with a comment before every line saying what the line does and why. Write your own version — in another language, as a spreadsheet, or with a different design. Python is free from python.org.7

# Basic COCOMO (Constructive Cost Model), organic mode: a short calculator you can rewrite in your own way.
# Run it with the size as the first argument, for example: python3 estimate.py 3.0
import sys
# The size S, in thousands of lines of code, is the first argument; 3.0 when none is given.
s = float(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 3.0
# Effort in person-months: E = 2.4 x S^1.05.
e = 2.4 * s ** 1.05
# Duration in months: D = 2.5 x E^0.38.
d = 2.5 * e ** 0.38
# Average staff in people: P = E / D.
p = e / d
# Print the three numbers with one decimal, as the lab asks.
print(f"S = {s:.1f}  E = {e:.1f} person-months  D = {d:.1f} months  P = {p:.1f} people")
# Capacity of the team: members x minutes per week x weeks, turned into person-months of 152 hours.
cap = 4 * 220 * 14 / 60 / 152
# The size this capacity covers, from the same formula solved for S: S = (E / 2.4)^(1 / 1.05).
print(f"capacity = {cap:.2f} person-months, which covers about {(cap / 2.4) ** (1 / 1.05):.2f} thousand lines")

Run it with python3 estimate.py 3.0 (on Windows, py estimate.py 3.0). For a size of 3.0 thousand lines it prints E = 7.6 person-months, D = 5.4 months, P = 1.4 people — the same numbers as the worked example. Change the capacity line to your team's real numbers.

Version notes

Everything shown was checked on October 5, 2026. If a newer version of a site or program looks or behaves differently, follow its official documentation.

  1. Git. The current release was 2.56.0, published September 28, 2026 (git-scm.com). The commands used here — add, commit, tag, push origin <tag> — have been stable for many years; the wording of Git's messages can differ slightly between versions. Why tags need their own push: Pro Git, “Tagging”.
  2. Where tags are listed. On GitHub, tags are under Releases → Tags (GitHub Docs — Viewing tags). GitHub changes its interface often; if the link has moved, search the repository page for “Tags”. GitLab, Codeberg and other hosts list tags in their own menus.
  3. Mermaid. The documentation showed Mermaid 12.1 (Mermaid — Gantt syntax). GitHub draws Mermaid charts inside Markdown (GitHub Docs — Creating diagrams) but may run a different version; writing info in a Mermaid block shows which. The chart in the template was tested with Mermaid 12.1.0.
  4. Visual Studio Code. Version 1.140 was released on September 30, 2026 (release notes); menus and the Markdown preview may look different in later versions. Any editor works.
  5. Copying a file. cp works in macOS and Linux terminals, in Git Bash and in Windows PowerShell; in the Windows Command Prompt the command is copy. Copying in the editor or the file manager is just as good.
  6. The course site. Each institution's LMS (Learning Management System) looks different; the post in the animation is a schematic, not a screenshot.
  7. Python. Python 3.14 was the current stable series on October 5, 2026, and Python 3.15.0 was scheduled for October 9, 2026 (the official release schedule). The example script runs on any Python 3.
  8. Drawing tools. draw.io, Excalidraw and spreadsheet programs change their menus often; none of them is required — a photographed paper timeline is accepted.
  9. About the animations. All seven were drawn for this course with a short program; the terminal and the hosting site are schematic, and Team Falcon, QueueLess and the address git.example.org (a domain reserved for examples) are fictional.
